problem.summary: YOLO-style detectors are efficient but can only detect a fixed set of categories seen during training, while existing open-vocabulary detectors rely on heavy backbones and online text encoding, making them computationally expensive and hard to deploy in real-world/edge scenarios.
statements: Trained detectors can only detect the specific categories defined and labeled at training time, limiting applicability in open scenarios.
Distillation-based open-vocabulary methods are limited by scarce training data with limited vocabulary diversity.
Large open-vocabulary detectors suffer from heavy computation burden and complicated deployment for edge devices.
Pre-training small detectors to endow them with open recognition capabilities remains unexplored.

evidence.quote: their reliance on predefined and trained object categories limits their applicability in open scenarios.
those methods still struggle for detection in realworld scenarios, which suffer from two aspects: (1) heavy computation burden and (2) complicated deployment for edge devices.
pre-training small detectors to endow them with open recognition capabilities remains unexplored.

background.summary: Builds on the YOLO family (YOLOv8/PAN, path-aggregation and re-parameterization designs) and on vision-language open-vocabulary detectors (GLIP, Grounding DINO, DetCLIP, GLIPv2, MDETR, ViLD, Detic) that reformulate detection as region-text matching; the claimed gap is that these methods use heavy detectors with Swin-L backbones and online text encoding, so small/efficient detectors pre-trained at scale were missing.

relatedWork.name: GLIP
relatedWork.relation: phrase-grounding pre-training framework for open-vocabulary detection
relatedWork.quote: GLIP [24] presents a pre-training framework for openvocabulary detection based on phrase grounding and evaluates in a zero-shot setting.

relatedWork.name: Grounding DINO
relatedWork.relation: integrates grounded pre-training into detection transformers with cross-modality fusion
relatedWork.quote: Grounding DINO [30] incorporates the grounded pre-training [24] into detection transformers [60] with cross-modality fusions.

relatedWork.name: YOLO series
relatedWork.relation: efficient one-stage architecture that YOLO-World extends to open vocabulary
relatedWork.quote: Several works [10, 23, 33, 52, 55] propose various architectures or designs for YOLO, including path aggregation networks [29], cross-stage partial networks [51], and re-parameterization [6], which further improve both speed and accuracy.

relatedWork.name: ZSD-YOLO
relatedWork.relation: only prior YOLO-based open-vocabulary attempt, aligned via language models
relatedWork.quote: Differing from ZSD-YOLO [54], which also explores open-vocabulary detection [58] with YOLO through language model alignment, YOLO-World introduces a novel YOLO framework with an effective pre-training strategy

evidence.quote: these methods often use heavy detectors like ATSS [61] or DINO [60] with Swin-L [32] as a backbone, leading to high computational demands and deployment challenges.
they only handle object detection with a fixed vocabulary, e.g., 80 categories in the COCO [26] dataset.

solution.summary: YOLO-World pairs a YOLOv8 detector with a frozen CLIP text encoder and a Re-parameterizable Vision-Language PAN (RepVL-PAN) for cross-modality fusion, trained with a region-text contrastive loss over detection, grounding, and pseudo-labeled image-text data; at deployment the text encoder is dropped and vocabulary embeddings are re-parameterized into network weights under a prompt-then-detect paradigm.
solution.approach: Reformulate detection annotations as region-text pairs, fuse text embeddings into multi-scale YOLO features with T-CSPLayer and Image-Pooling Attention, and re-parameterize offline vocabulary embeddings into the detector weights for fast inference.
components: Image-Pooling Attention for image-aware text embeddings
text contrastive head with L2-normalized region-text similarity
region-text contrastive loss combined with IoU loss and distributed focal loss
prompt-then-detect offline vocabulary re-parameterized into layer weights
pseudo-labeling pipeline (n-gram noun extraction, GLIP boxes, CLIP filtering)

evidence.quote: an innovative approach that enhances YOLO with openvocabulary detection capabilities through vision-language modeling and pre-training on large-scale datasets.
During inference, the text encoder can be removed and the text embeddings can be re-parameterized into weights of RepVL-PAN for efficient deployment.
we present a prompt-then-detect strategy with an offline vocabulary for further efficiency.
we sample and label 246k images from CC3M [47] with 821k pseudo annotations.

experiments.summary: Pre-trained 100 epochs on Objects365, GoldG (GQA/Flickr30k) and pseudo-labeled CC3M, then evaluated zero-shot on LVIS minival (Fixed AP) and COCO, fine-tuned for COCO/LVIS detection and open-vocabulary instance segmentation, with ablations over pre-training data, RepVL-PAN components, and text encoders; speed measured on a single NVIDIA V100.

evidence.quote: On the challenging LVIS dataset, YOLO-World achieves 35.4 AP with 52.0 FPS on V100, which outperforms many state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed.
YOLO-World-L outperforms YOLOv8-L by 7.2 AP and 10.2 APr
the proposed RepVL-PAN improves the baseline (YOLOv8-PAN [20]) by 1.1 AP on LVIS

limitations.summary: The authors note that fine-tuning all modules for closed-set performance can erode zero-shot ability, that fine-tuning the CLIP text encoder severely hurts performance, and that excessive pseudo-labeled image-text data can hurt the smallest model.
items: Fine-tuning all modules degrades open-vocabulary performance (0.6 box APr drop for YOLO-World-L).
Fine-tuning the CLIP text encoder during pre-training causes a severe performance drop (attributed to O365's limited vocabulary).
Excessive pseudo-labeled image-text data has negative effects for small models (YOLO-World-S).
Removing RepVL-PAN for COCO fine-tuning limits vision-language interaction to small vocabularies.
Reported speed depends on the re-parameterized/offline-vocabulary setting and hardware (single V100).

evidence.quote: the fine-tuning might degrade the open-vocabulary performance and lead to a 0.6 box APr drop for YOLO-World-L.
while fine-tuning CLIP leads to a severe performance drop.
using an excessive amount of pseudo-labeled data may have some negative effects for small models

futureDirections.direction: Study what data is needed to pre-train small models / YOLO detectors at scale.
futureDirections.quote: We will explore more about the data for pre-training small models or YOLO detectors in future work.

futureDirections.direction: Position YOLO-World as a benchmark for real-world open-vocabulary detection and release code/weights for practical applications.
futureDirections.quote: We hope YOLO-World can serve as a new benchmark for addressing real-world open-vocabulary detection.

algorithms: re-parameterization of text embeddings into conv/linear weights

applications.detail: Object detection is framed as serving image understanding, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.
applications.quote: Object detection has been a long-standing and fundamental challenge in computer vision with numerous applications in image understanding, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.

applications.detail: Prompt-then-detect with an offline vocabulary lets users pre-encode categories and re-parameterize them into model weights, removing the text encoder at inference for easier deployment on edge devices.
Fine-tuned YOLO-World transfers to open-vocabulary instance segmentation and referring/referring-style object detection with user-defined vocabularies.
applications.quote: the fine-tuned YOLO-World achieves remarkable performance on several downstream tasks, including object detection and openvocabulary instance segmentation.

deploymentClaims: 35.4 AP with 52.0 FPS on an NVIDIA V100 (re-parameterized, w/o TensorRT).
YOLO-World-S has 13M parameters while still supporting vision-language pre-training.
Fine-tuned YOLO-World-L reaches 53.3 AP on COCO val2017 at 156 FPS with TensorRT.
Text encoder removed at inference; offline vocabulary embeddings folded into network weights.

evidence.quote: we measure the inference speeds of all models on one NVIDIA V100 GPU without extra acceleration mechanisms, e.g., FP16 or TensorRT.
During inference, the text encoder can be removed and the text embeddings can be re-parameterized into weights of RepVL-PAN for efficient deployment.
